title: What is the structure of a JWT — Header (algorithm + type) + Payload (claims: sub, exp, iat, custom) + Signature (HMAC or RSA) — and why is the payload NOT encrypted (only Base64-encoded, anyone can read it)?
shortTitle: Structure of a JWT (Header, Payload, Signature) and Why the Payload Is Not Encrypted

s1_definition.profdef: A JWT (JSON Web Token) is a compact, URL-safe token made of three Base64Url-encoded parts separated by dots: a Header describing the signing algorithm and token type, a Payload carrying claims (standard ones like sub, exp, iat, iss plus custom claims), and a Signature computed over the header and payload using either a symmetric secret (HMAC) or an asymmetric private key (RSA/ECDSA). The signature guarantees integrity and authenticity but not confidentiality — the payload is only encoded, not encrypted, so anyone can decode and read it.
s1_definition.analogy: A JWT is like a cheque from National Bank of India. The top corner says what kind of cheque and which signing method the bank uses (header). The body shows the payee and amount — Rajesh, account SAV2001, valid until 5pm (payload). The bottom has the bank's signature (signature). Anyone who finds the cheque can READ the payee and amount; the signature does not hide anything, it only proves the bank really wrote it and nobody altered it. That is why you never write a secret PIN on a cheque.
s1_definition.oneliner: A JWT is signed, not sealed — the signature proves it is genuine and untampered, but everyone can read the payload.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A JWT (JSON Web Token) is a compact, URL-safe token made of three Base64Url-encoded parts separated by dots: a Header describing the signing algorithm and token type, a Payload carrying claims (standard ones like sub, exp, iat, iss plus custom claims), and a Signature computed over the header and payload using either a symmetric secret (HMAC) or an asymmetric private key (RSA/ECDSA). The signature guarantees integrity and authenticity but not confidentiality — the payload is only encoded, not encrypted, so anyone can decode and read it.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** A JWT is like a cheque from National Bank of India. The top corner says what kind of cheque and which signing method the bank uses (header). The body shows the payee and amount — Rajesh, account SAV2001, valid until 5pm (payload). The bottom has the bank's signature (signature). Anyone who finds the cheque can READ the payee and amount; the signature does not hide anything, it only proves the bank really wrote it and nobody altered it. That is why you never write a secret PIN on a cheque.

**One line to remember:** A JWT is signed, not sealed — the signature proves it is genuine and untampered, but everyone can read the payload.

sections.s2_technical:
The header is a tiny JSON object such as `{"alg":"HS256","typ":"JWT"}`, Base64Url-encoded to form the first segment. It tells the verifier which algorithm to use. The payload is a JSON object of claims, for example `{"sub":"rajesh","role":"CUSTOMER","iat":1730000000,"exp":1730000900,"iss":"national-bank"}`, Base64Url-encoded to form the second segment. Standard registered claims include sub (subject/user), exp (expiry), iat (issued-at), iss (issuer), aud (audience), and jti (token id).

The signature is computed over the already-encoded header and payload joined by a dot. For HMAC it is `HMACSHA256(base64Url(header) + "." + base64Url(payload), secret)`; for RSA it is a signature made with the issuer's private key and verified with the public key. The final token is `header.payload.signature`. If even one byte of the payload changes, recomputing the signature no longer matches, so tampering is detected. For example, a verifier does `Jwts.parser().verifyWith(key).build().parseSignedClaims(token)` which throws on a bad signature.

The crucial senior point is why the payload is not encrypted. Base64Url is an encoding, not encryption — there is no key, so anyone can reverse it instantly. The signature protects integrity (it was not changed) and authenticity (it came from the issuer), not confidentiality. Therefore you must never place secrets, passwords, full card numbers, or balances in a JWT payload. If you genuinely need confidentiality you use JWE (JSON Web Encryption), which actually encrypts the payload, but plain JWTs (JWS) are the common case.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India issues Rajesh a token after login. Every microservice must be able to confirm the token is genuine and unaltered without calling back to the login server. This is exactly how the JWT signature works — each service recomputes the signature with the shared key and trusts the token only if it matches.

Problem 2 — A developer is tempted to store Rajesh's account balance and PIN inside the token "to save a database call." But because the payload is only Base64-encoded, anyone who captures the token can read those values instantly. This is exactly why the payload must never hold secrets — encoding is not encryption.

Our mini-project builds a `JwtCodec` that assembles header, payload, and signature; the demo prints the three parts, decodes the payload in plain sight to prove readability, verifies a good token, and shows that flipping a payload byte breaks the signature while the attacker could still read the old payload.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a header JSON, a payload JSON with sub "rajesh" and role "CUSTOMER", and a signing secret.

Step 1: `create` Base64Url-encodes the header to form segment one and the payload to form segment two. Nothing is hidden — these are reversible encodings.

Step 2: `create` signs the string "segment1.segment2" with HMAC-SHA256 and the secret, producing segment three. The final JWT is the three segments joined by dots.

Step 3: The demo splits the JWT and decodes segments one and two back to readable JSON, proving anyone can read the claims. The signature segment is opaque but still not secret — it protects integrity, not confidentiality.

Step 4: `verify` recomputes the signature over the first two segments and compares to segment three; it matches, so the token is genuine. Then the demo tampers the payload to role ADMIN and re-encodes it, keeping the old signature. Now the recomputed signature no longer matches, so `verify` returns false — tampering is detected even though the attacker could read and alter the plaintext payload.

```text
2026-10-31 22:50:00.010 INFO    [JwtStructureDemo] JWT = eyJhbGci...eyJzdWIi...Xq9...
2026-10-31 22:50:00.011 INFO    [JwtStructureDemo] Header  (segment 1) = {"alg":"HS256","typ":"JWT"}
2026-10-31 22:50:00.012 INFO    [JwtStructureDemo] Payload (segment 2) = {"sub":"rajesh","role":"CUSTOMER",...}
2026-10-31 22:50:00.013 WARNING [JwtStructureDemo] Payload is only Base64-decoded, readable by anyone -> never put secrets here
2026-10-31 22:50:00.014 INFO    [JwtStructureDemo] Signature valid? true
2026-10-31 22:50:00.015 SEVERE  [JwtStructureDemo] Tampered token signature valid? false
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  Build JWT
    │
    ├─ Header  {"alg":"HS256","typ":"JWT"}  ──base64url──→ segment 1
    ├─ Payload {"sub":"rajesh","exp":...}   ──base64url──→ segment 2
    │
    ▼
  sign(segment1 + "." + segment2, secret)  ──→ segment 3
    │
    ▼
  JWT = segment1.segment2.segment3
    │
    ├─ VERIFY PATH                    ├─ TAMPER PATH
    │  recompute sig over 1.2         │  attacker edits payload (role=ADMIN)
    │  equals segment3? genuine     │  recomputed sig != old segment3
    ▼                                 ▼
  trust claims                       reject (integrity broken)
  (note: payload READABLE either way — not encrypted)
```

sections.s5d_lld:
```text
  ═══ LLD — JwtCodec ═══

  ┌──────────────────────────────┐
  │          JwtCodec            │
  │ ──────────────────────────── │
  │ - secret: String             │
  │ ──────────────────────────── │
  │ + create(header,payload):    │  → "h.p.s"
  │     String                   │
  │ + verify(jwt): boolean       │  recompute sig, compare
  │ + decode(segment): String    │  base64url → plaintext (readable!)
  │ - sign(data): String         │  HMAC-SHA256
  │ - enc(s): String             │  base64url encode
  └──────────────────────────────┘

  Token anatomy:
    header   = base64url({"alg","typ"})      ← readable
    payload  = base64url({sub,exp,iat,iss})  ← readable (NOT encrypted)
    signature= HMAC/RSA over header.payload  ← proves integrity+authenticity

  Contract for verify(jwt):
    Post: true only if recomputed signature == provided signature
    Note: confidentiality NOT provided — use JWE if payload must be secret
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
A JWT is a compact token with three Base64Url-encoded parts separated by dots. The header names the algorithm and token type, the payload carries claims such as sub for the subject, exp for expiry, iat for issued-at, iss for issuer, plus any custom claims like role, and the signature is computed over the header and payload using either an HMAC secret or an RSA private key. The signature is what makes the token trustworthy: if anyone changes a single byte of the header or payload, the recomputed signature will not match and the token is rejected.

In my banking project each microservice verifies the signature locally with the shared key, so it can trust a token without calling back to the login server. In my demo I showed assembling the three parts, verifying a genuine token, and then tampering with the payload to escalate the role to ADMIN — the signature check immediately failed, which is exactly the integrity protection we rely on.

The point I always stress is why the payload is not encrypted. Base64Url is only an encoding, not encryption; there is no key, so anyone who captures the token can decode and read every claim instantly. The signature protects integrity and authenticity, meaning the token was not altered and really came from the issuer, but it provides zero confidentiality.

That is why in a bank I never put secrets, passwords, full card numbers, or balances in a JWT payload — I keep it to an identifier, a role, and expiry, and fetch sensitive data from the database behind proper authorization. If a payload genuinely must be confidential I use JWE, which actually encrypts it, but for normal stateless auth a signed JWT with a short expiry and no secrets in the claims is the right design.

---

keyPoints: JWT: Header.Payload.Signature — Base64 encoded, not encrypted
Signature verifies integrity — payload is readable by anyone
Access token: short-lived (15 min). Refresh token: long-lived (days)
Store in HttpOnly cookie (XSS-safe), never in localStorage
